newsitem.title: USA: Legendary centenarian still picking stocks.
newsitem.headline: Legendary centenarian still picking stocks.

text.p: Born the same year as the Dow Jones industrial average was created and one of the forefathers of the mutual fund, Philip Carret believes U.S. stocks have at least another 100 good years left.
Credited by market guru Warren Buffett as having "the best long-term investment record in America," Carret says his secret to success is straightforward: keep it simple.

In 1928, Carret quit his job as an economist and created a new investment vehicle, a mutual fund. A $10,000 investment in his Fidelity Investment Trust, renamed Pioneer Fund in 1951, would be worth more than $41.7 million now.

"I think the United States, like all great empires, will probably collapse, but that's at least 100, probably 200 years away," he said at a birthday celebration in Boston. "In the meantime, why, there's great opportunity."
On Nov. 29, Carret will celebrate his 100th birthday, which he has "celebrated" for the past eight years, and he will finally cut back his working week from five eight-hour days.
Carret believes investors who try to time the markets are crazy, but nevertheless thinks stocks are due for a correction of 1,000 to 2,000 points, as measured on the 30-share Dow industrial average.
But there is no reason to panic, he says, which is not surprising from someone who has worked through more than 30 bull markets, 31 bear markets and 20 recessions, not to mention the Depression.
Always humble, Carret said there were no market experts, only market professionals, and anyone can read a corporate annual report or investigate a company.
"The most important thing in investing is to use common sense. If it's not a simple concept, why I leave it alone personally," he said.
He stays away from high-technology companies and only invests in companies with products he understands.

"What is the simplest, simplest company in the market? Coca-Cola. It takes from my standpoint a terrible tasting substance and sells it by the billions of gallons, I guess, and is one of the most successful companies in the world," he said.

His all-time favourite stock is a little-known packaging company called Greif Bros Corp., based in Delaware, Ohio, recommended to him by an Omaha stockbroker, Howard Buffett, Warren's father, in 1946.
He decided to invest in Greif Bros. after management stressed in its annual report the negatives when, in fact, the business was "growing like weeds."

"One thing I like to see in an annual report is emphasis on the negative if the results are good. If the management is cheering for itself in a big way and the results aren't quite that good, I don't want any part of it," he said.
Today, Carret works as a portfolio manager at Carret & Co., a New York money managment firm that he founded in 1963.

"I am going to semi-retire at the end of the year, maybe cut my working schedule down to two or three days a week," he said. "As long as I'm physically able, my mind seems to be working reasonably well, I expect to keep on going."
